assessment.nobel_worthiness: Predicting and then finding a new topological phase of band insulators, with protected edge states and a quantized response, is the clearest example of experiment and theory jointly revealing a new state of matter in a solid. The impact has been deep and lasting across materials physics and spectroscopy (ARPES), and the concept is now a standard part of electronic-structure theory.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental realization in HgTe wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The supplied credit supports a clean theory-plus-experiment trio. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D insulator contributors are not in the credited names, so some allocation is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed in many materials and platforms for nearly two decades, including angle-resolved photoemission for the 3D case. The interpretation is stable and recognition is timely, even somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: The 2D quantum spin Hall realisation and the 3D topological insulators are partly separate discoveries, and the credit across them is not cleanly split.
I rely on my own recollection of the HgTe experiments and the prediction chronology, not on a fresh check.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and the very large effect with MgO barriers, is a spin-dependent quantum transport phenomenon with a clear physical origin in band-structure and symmetry filtering of tunnelling electrons. It is also the basis of read heads and magnetic memory, so the work links fundamental magnetism to practical technology, which suits the theme of quantum mechanics as a foundation for devices.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported room-temperature TMR in 1995. Parkin's group, with Yuasa and colleagues, reported the giant MgO effect in 2004, and theory by Butler and Mathon predicted the coherent tunnelling. Not all of these people are in the credited set, so a three-person prize leaves out decisive contributors. The credited trio is defensible but not complete.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, reproduced in many laboratories and in commercial devices for about two decades. Theory of coherent tunnelling quantitatively matches experiment, which I value. The field was already close to the 2007 GMR prize, so the novelty of the step beyond it may be debated.
uncertainties: Attribution between the 1995 and 2004 MgO discoveries and the theorists who predicted symmetry filtering is contested.
The overlap with the 2007 GMR prize could be read as an incremental advance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory made the quantitative treatment of strongly correlated electrons tractable, giving a controlled description of the Mott transition and, combined with DFT, of real correlated materials. This is the theory most directly connected to my own field, and it has changed how spectra of correlated materials are computed and understood.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar built the mapping onto an impurity problem, and Müller-Hartmann and Jarrell, among others, were also important. Vollhardt, Georges and Kotliar form a plausible trio, but the origins in the infinite-dimension limit make the split of credit imperfect.
assessment.maturity: Widely used and confirmed against experimental spectra for thirty years, and DFT+DMFT is now standard practice. Prize-worthy as a method, but I would ask whether the Committee prefers a physical discovery over a computational framework.
uncertainties: The Committee may prefer a discovery about nature to a theoretical method, even a very influential one.
Credit in the foundational papers is shared with people outside the credited set, e.g. Metzner and Müller-Hartmann; I am recalling this from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle, followed by observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, opened moire quantum materials as a platform with tunable strong correlations. This is exactly the kind of new quantum behaviour in a material that I find compelling, and the field has grown enormously.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 continuum-model prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experiments. Cao, the first author of those papers, and others such as Dean (hBN encapsulation) and Santos and Lopes dos Santos, are not in the credited names, so this raises a real attribution question.
assessment.maturity: Observation of the correlated phases has been reproduced by several groups, but the nature of the superconducting pairing and the role of strain, disorder and twist-angle inhomogeneity remain debated. Recognition may be somewhat early, though the core observations are solid.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism is unresolved and theory does not yet explain the full phase diagram.
The credited set omits the experimental first author and other contributors, and the experimental and theory parts may merit different recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showing that long-range magnetic order survives in atomically thin crystals (CrI3 and Cr2Ge2Te6) settled a question that standard theory had framed through the Mermin-Wagner theorem, and the role of anisotropy. This relates directly to my work on magnetism in 2D and van der Waals systems, and opens new device concepts with electrical control of magnetism.
assessment.attribution: The two 2017 papers, one from Xu's group on CrI3 and one from Zhang's group on Cr2Ge2Te6, are the parallel decisive experiments, and the credited names cover them. Jarillo-Herrero (also credited) was a co-author on the CrI3 work but his case is stronger in other candidates, so I propose Xu and Zhang only.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups and materials, with extensive theoretical modelling, but the field is less than ten years old and the subsequent device implementations are still developing. Timely but possibly early.
uncertainties: Maturity: the long-term importance of 2D magnets is not yet clear.
Zhang's group reported its result in parallel with Xu's, so attribution should be checked against the original papers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of superconductivity in organic Bechgaard salts, the first superconductors of this type, revealed unconventional superconducting and spin-density-wave phases in low-dimensional correlated systems. It anticipated key themes of later unconventional superconductors and is a clean, original materials discovery with a clear physical interpretation.
assessment.attribution: Bechgaard synthesised the materials and Jérome's group demonstrated superconductivity under pressure in 1980; the two names represent the discovery well. Others in the team, notably Parkin, Ribault and Mailly, could be an allocation question, but I am not sure how credit was recorded.
assessment.maturity: Four decades of confirmation and theory, though the pairing mechanism is still debated. The prize is arguably overdue, and the age of the laureates is a practical concern for timing.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee views this as a sufficiently broad impact beyond one family of materials.
The pairing mechanism remains debated, and the full credit within the original team is uncertain from my memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Observing the quantum anomalous Hall effect, a quantized Hall conductance with no external magnetic field, in magnetic topological insulator films is an elegant demonstration of topological physics in a magnetic material. It builds on the topological insulator idea and on the theory of the effect, and is a precise and reproducible quantum phenomenon.
assessment.attribution: Theory by Fang, Dai and collaborators (including Haldane's earlier model, which is already recognised) predicted the effect in Cr- or Mn-doped materials, and Xue's group made the 2013 observation. Chang and others in that group are not in the credited names. The trio is plausible but allocation remains unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by other groups, with temperatures and precision still improving, so the effect is robust though the experimental scope is still evolving. It would be stronger after the topological insulator prize, as it builds on it.
uncertainties: Overlaps conceptually with a topological insulator prize and would likely follow that rather than precede it.
Low operating temperatures and sample disorder issues remain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, observed the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and fermionic correlations, and made a quantum simulator for many-body physics. It reveals new quantum behaviour and gives theorists a controlled test bed for the models I care about in solids.
assessment.attribution: Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition in 2002 following the Jaksch, Zoller proposal, and Esslinger's group did the fermionic Hubbard work. Zoller is credited but I leave him out of this ballot slot because the proposal is only part of the story; this is a judgement and could be debated. Several other experimental leaders are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed in many laboratories, with the field maturing and quantum simulation now a mainstream effort. The area is somewhat close to the prizes already given for cold-atom physics (BEC, laser cooling).
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier atomic physics prizes and the question of which part of the lattice work is the discovery.
Possible omission of Zoller's role in the original proposal; the choice of laureates is uncertain.
